title: Module Documentation and Approach
content:
The module docstring surveys the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra: every non-constant polynomial over $\mathbb{C}$ has a root. The core result (`Complex.exists_root`) comes from Mathlib, proved via Liouville's theorem from complex analysis. This file contributes pedagogical exposition, the contrapositive formulation, root-counting, complete factorization, and a worked quadratic case.

Despite its name, FTA is fundamentally analytic — every known proof relies on completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{C}$). The Mathlib proof uses: $p$ has no roots $\Rightarrow$ $1/p$ is bounded entire $\Rightarrow$ $1/p$ is constant (Liouville) $\Rightarrow$ $p$ is constant — contradiction.
mathContext: The four imports provide the complete toolkit: `Analysis.Complex.Polynomial.Basic` for `Complex.exists_root` (FTA), `Polynomial.Basic` and `Degree.Definitions` for polynomial API, `IsAlgClosed.Basic` for the algebraic closure instance `Complex.isAlgClosed` and `Splits`.

title: Worked Examples: z² + 1
content:
Two concrete examples demonstrating Lean's polynomial API: (1) `degree (X^2 + 1) = 2` is verified using `degree_add_eq_left_of_degree_lt`, showing the higher-degree term dominates; (2) `IsRoot (X^2 + 1) I` — the imaginary unit $i$ is a root, verified by `simp` with `Complex.I_sq` ($i^2 = -1$) and `norm_num`.

These examples motivate the general theorem: $z^2 + 1$ has no real roots but has complex roots $\pm i$. The FTA guarantees such roots always exist for non-constant polynomials.
mathContext: $z^2 + 1 = (z - i)(z + i)$, so $i$ is a root: $i^2 + 1 = -1 + 1 = 0$. This is the simplest polynomial requiring complex numbers.

title: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
content:
`fundamental_theorem_of_algebra`: every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has at least one complex root. The proof is a one-liner delegating to Mathlib's `Complex.exists_root`.

This is Wiedijk's #2 on the list of 100 Greatest Theorems. Despite its algebraic statement, every known proof uses analytic or topological properties of $\mathbb{C}$: Liouville's theorem (Mathlib's approach), winding numbers, Galois theory + intermediate value theorem, or the maximum modulus principle.
mathContext: $\forall p \in \mathbb{C}[z],\, \deg p \geq 1 \implies \exists z_0 \in \mathbb{C},\, p(z_0) = 0$. Equivalently: $\mathbb{C}$ is algebraically closed.

title: Contrapositive: No Roots Implies Constant
content:
`no_roots_implies_constant`: if $p(z) 
eq 0$ for all $z \in \mathbb{C}$, then $\deg p = 0$ (i.e., $p$ is constant). This is the contrapositive of FTA and sometimes the more convenient formulation.

The proof uses `by_contra` to assume $\deg p 
eq 0$, splits on $p = 0$ vs $p 
eq 0$ (the zero polynomial has every element as a root, contradicting the hypothesis), then shows $\deg p > 0$ and applies FTA to find a root — contradicting the no-roots hypothesis.
mathContext:
$( orall z \in \mathbb{C},\, p(z) 
eq 0) \Rightarrow \deg p = 0$. This is logically equivalent to FTA by contraposition: $
eg(\exists z,\, p(z) = 0) \Rightarrow 
eg(\deg p \geq 1)$.

title: Algebraic Closure and Complete Splitting
content:
`Complex.isAlgClosed` is Mathlib's instance asserting $\mathbb{C}$ is algebraically closed. `splits_over_complex` applies `IsAlgClosed.splits_codomain` to show every polynomial splits completely into linear factors over $\mathbb{C}$.

'Splitting' means $p(z) = c \prod_{i}(z - r_i)$ where the $r_i$ are the roots. This is the factorization-theoretic restatement of FTA: not only does a root exist, but repeated root extraction decomposes $p$ entirely.
mathContext: $\mathbb{C}$ is algebraically closed $\iff$ every $p \in \mathbb{C}[z]$ splits into linear factors. `Splits f p` in Mathlib means $p.\text{map}(f)$ is a product of linear factors. With $f = \text{id}_{\mathbb{C}}$, this gives the splitting over $\mathbb{C}$ itself.

title: Root Count Equals Degree
content:
`card_roots_eq_degree`: for a non-zero polynomial $p \in \mathbb{C}[z]$, the number of roots (counted with multiplicity) equals the degree. The proof uses `IsAlgClosed.splits_codomain` to get splitting, then `natDegree_eq_card_roots` to count roots from the factorization.

Mathlib represents roots as a `Multiset` (a list up to permutation), where multiplicity is encoded by repetition. `Multiset.card` counts with multiplicity.
mathContext: $|\text{roots}(p)| = \deg p$ for $p \neq 0$. Example: $z^3 - z^2 = z^2(z-1)$ has $\text{roots} = \{0, 0, 1\}$, $|\text{roots}| = 3 = \deg p$.

title: Monic Polynomial Complete Factorization
content:
`monic_prod_roots`: a monic polynomial $p$ equals $\prod_{r \in \text{roots}(p)} (X - r)$. This is the canonical factorization for monic polynomials over algebraically closed fields.

The proof establishes splitting via `IsAlgClosed.splits_codomain`, obtains the root count via `natDegree_eq_card_roots`, then invokes Mathlib's `prod_multiset_X_sub_C_of_monic_of_roots_card_eq` — the theorem that a monic polynomial with matching root count equals the product of its linear factors.
mathContext: For monic $p$: $p(z) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}(z - r_i)$ where $r_1, \ldots, r_n$ are roots with multiplicity. Combined with Vieta's formulas, this gives $a_{n-1} = -(r_1 + \cdots + r_n)$, $a_0 = (-1)^n r_1 \cdots r_n$.

title: Quadratic Case: Every Quadratic Has Roots
content:
`quadratic_has_root`: for $a, b, c \in \mathbb{C}$ with $a \neq 0$, there exists $z$ with $az^2 + bz + c = 0$. The proof constructs the polynomial $p = C(a) \cdot X^2 + C(b) \cdot X + C(c)$, shows $\deg p = 2 > 0$ (a non-trivial calculation requiring `degree_add_eq_left_of_degree_lt` and careful degree estimates for each term), then applies FTA.

The degree computation is the longest part of the proof (lines 181-201) because polynomial degree in Lean is defined as a `WithBot ℕ` (natural numbers with $-\infty$), requiring careful handling of the zero cases and comparison with the `degree_C` and `degree_X_pow` lemmas.
mathContext: The classical quadratic formula $z = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$ gives roots explicitly. Over $\mathbb{C}$, the discriminant $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$ always has a square root (since $\mathbb{C}$ is algebraically closed), so complex roots always exist. The FTA proof here is more general: it doesn't need to exhibit the root, only to prove existence.
